### **Possession, Bailments, and Gifts of Personal Property**

**High-Level Overview**

* Ownership of unowned or escaped property generally turns on **possession**, especially whether a claimant has established actual or legally recognized control.
* Courts may replace a strict **property rule** with a **liability rule** when competing claims and wrongful third-party conduct make an all-or-nothing award inequitable.
* A **bailment** arises when one person has custody of another’s personal property; the bailee must return the property and exercise the level of care reasonable under the circumstances.
* A valid **inter vivos gift** requires **present donative intent**, **delivery**, and **acceptance**; a mere promise of a future or testamentary transfer ordinarily is unenforceable outside a will.
* **Actual delivery**, **constructive delivery**, and **symbolic delivery** are alternative methods of completing a gift, but courts scrutinize whether the chosen method genuinely demonstrates a present transfer of the particular property interest claimed.

**Finder’s Rights, the True Owner, and Avoiding Double Liability**

* A central policy of **finder’s law** is returning lost property to its **true owner**; accordingly, the true owner’s claim remains superior to a finder’s claim.
* If a defendant has already paid the finder the property’s full value in **trover**, but the true owner later demands the property, the legal system should try to avoid imposing **double liability** on the defendant.
* The defendant ordinarily may **implead** the finder who received the earlier damages and require that person to return the recovery to the available pool of compensation.
* This solution prevents the finder from retaining a windfall after the true owner establishes a superior claim.
* If the finder has already dissipated the damages, resolution becomes more complicated because the funds may no longer be recoverable.
* **Replevin** would not work if the defendant cannot return or account for the actual item; in that circumstance, payment of the item’s value through **trover** becomes the relevant remedy.

**_Armory v. Delamirie_, Court and Year Not Supplied**

* **Context**
  * The court awarded Armory **trover** for the value of the ring or its jewels.
  * The lecture considered a variation in which Delamirie still possessed the ring after paying Armory damages and the true owner later appeared.
* **Rule and Application**
  * The true owner would have priority and could demand the ring.
  * To prevent **double liability**, Delamirie could **implead** Armory and seek to return Armory’s earlier recovery to the compensation pool.
  * If Armory had already dissipated the recovery, the otherwise clean solution would become more difficult.

**Possession of Unowned Property and the Role of Control**

* For wild animals and analogous unowned objects, ownership ordinarily arises when a claimant establishes **control**.
* When rival hunters or whaling ships pursue the same animal, courts generally favor the party who played the greatest role in establishing full control or had the greatest likelihood of completing capture.
* Merely beginning pursuit, wounding an animal, or temporarily slowing it generally does not defeat a later claimant who actually kills or captures it.
* The control inquiry may recognize either **actual control** or sufficiently strong **metaphorical control**, depending on custom, regulation, and the nature of the property.
* The professor emphasized that the baseball dispute discussed below appears in the theoretical-property and wild-animal materials, rather than solely in the finder materials, because the central issue is control rather than an ordinary accidental finding.

**_Popov v. Hayashi_, Court Not Supplied (Litigation Following a 2001 Game)**

* **Facts**
  * During a 2001 San Francisco baseball game, Barry Bonds hit a historically significant home-run ball into the right-field stands.
  * Popov positioned himself with a glove and initially caught or nearly caught the ball.
  * A crowd tackled or engulfed Popov, and the ball came out of his glove amid the commotion.
  * It was uncertain whether Popov would have retained the ball absent the crowd’s wrongful conduct.
  * Hayashi, who was not implicated in the crowd’s misconduct, stood near the outskirts, picked up the loose ball, and reduced it to complete control.
  * The ball ultimately sold for approximately $450,000.
* **Procedural History**
  * Popov sued Hayashi, asserting claims that included **conversion**, **trespass to chattels**, and requests for equitable relief, although the transcript is unclear about the complete list of claims.
* **Issue**
  * Did Popov acquire a legally protected **possessory interest** when he attempted to catch the ball but lost control because of the crowd’s wrongful conduct, even though Hayashi later obtained complete and innocent control?
* **Holding**
  * Yes. Popov had a legally cognizable interest arising from his interrupted attempt to establish control, while Hayashi also had a legitimate claim based on his complete and innocent possession; the court divided the ball’s value between them.
* **Reasoning**
  * **Conversion** is the wrongful exercise of dominion over another’s personal property, so the claim depended on whether Popov had acquired a property interest before Hayashi obtained the ball.
  * **Trespass to chattels** concerns damage to personal property or interference with the plaintiff’s use of it; it was not a useful fit because Hayashi neither damaged the ball nor participated in the crowd’s misconduct.
  * Barry Bonds had no ownership claim to the ball merely because he hit it.
  * The ball initially belonged to Major League Baseball or the stadium, but the governing policy treated balls leaving the field as abandoned to the spectators; Major League Baseball therefore had no continuing claim.
  * Hayashi was the first person who unquestionably reduced the ball to complete control.
  * Popov might have completed possession but for wrongful mob behavior.
  * Awarding the ball entirely to Hayashi would risk condoning a free-for-all in which crowds could improve the chances of obtaining valuable objects through violence.
  * Recognizing Popov’s partial interest protected his right to make an orderly attempt to catch the ball and discouraged mob behavior without punishing the innocent Hayashi.
  * The court effectively replaced an all-or-nothing **property rule** with a **liability rule**, converting the dispute into a distributional question resolved through money.
  * This approach reflected the rise of liability-rule analysis associated in the lecture with Calabresi and modern property jurisprudence.
  * The professor acknowledged a counterargument that dividing the value could be viewed as a judicial “cop out,” but explained that it could instead be understood as a modern response to overlapping entitlements.
* **Policy**
  * The opinion balanced protection of traditional possession principles against deterrence of wrongful crowd behavior.
  * The court’s subtext was that Popov and Hayashi should have cooperated, sold the ball, or arranged a buyout rather than incur years of litigation.
  * Any special subjective value to a collector or museum such as Cooperstown could be reflected through the market price; a claimant who valued the ball more could buy out the other claimant.

**Wild Animals, Domesticated Animals, and Escaped Property**

* **Wild deer hypothetical**
  * A wild deer roams on A’s land, but B places a feeding station on B’s land, lures the deer across the boundary, and kills it.
  * A had not established ownership merely because the wild deer happened to be on A’s land.
  * B established control by killing the deer, at which point it became a **chattel** under B’s control.
  * A therefore would not recover **trover** under the common-law possession rule, although a hunting statute or regulation might alter the result.
* **Domesticated dog variation**
  * If the animal is A’s domesticated dog rather than a wild deer, A has already established ownership through **domestication** and factual control.
  * Formal paperwork is not essential if the facts establish that the dog belongs to A.
  * B’s wrongful detention or interference would support **conversion** and liability for damages.
  * A may be responsible for damage caused by the dog, by an analogy to **respondeat superior** or agency, but A correspondingly retains the right to prevent neighbors from interfering with the animal.
* **Fenced-land variation**
  * If B cuts a hole in A’s fence and lures the enclosed deer out, B’s affirmative interference would support **wrongful conversion**.
  * If the deer independently finds a hole and escapes, A ordinarily loses control and does not retain the same claim.
* **Caged-deer variation**
  * If A captures a deer and places it in a cage, A has established actual control.
  * If the deer escapes on its own and reaches B’s property, A loses that actual control under the lecture’s analysis.
* **Identification variation**
  * Branding a horse or cow is an accepted method of establishing title and may constitute legally recognized or metaphorical control.
  * An ear tag or brand on a wild deer presents a close question whose resolution may depend on local custom or regulation.

**Bailments: Creation, Return, and Standards of Care**

* A **bailment** occurs when an owner, the **bailor**, transfers custody of personal property to another person, the **bailee**, without transferring ownership.
* A **voluntary bailment** arises when the owner intentionally places the property in another’s custody.
* An **involuntary bailment** arises when a finder takes custody of lost property even though the true owner did not select the finder.
* A bailee generally must return the property whenever the true owner requests it, unless an express loan agreement permits the bailee to retain it for a defined period.
* The recurring legal issue is the degree of care the bailee must exercise.
* Traditional law divided bailments according to who benefited:
  1. A bailment benefiting only the bailor imposed a relatively low duty on the bailee. A finder who safeguards lost property is doing the owner a favor, so the owner will have difficulty recovering if the finder accidentally loses it again.
  1. A bailment benefiting only the bailee imposed a high standard of care. A neighbor who borrows and carelessly loses or damages a lawn mower may be liable for its value or repair.
  1. A **mutual-benefit bailment** imposed an intermediate or ordinary-care obligation. Examples include a compensated commercial arrangement or an exchange in which both parties receive some benefit.
* Modern law tends to replace these rigid categories with a continuum requiring **reasonable care under the circumstances**.

**Valet-Parking Bailment Hypothetical**

* **Facts**
  * The professor paid a hotel approximately $50 per night for valet parking.
  * The hotel initially could not locate the rental car and found it approximately four hours after it was needed.
  * The valet staff had left the lights on, draining the battery and preventing the key fob from operating.
  * The staff did not record each parking space and instead ordinarily located vehicles by pressing the fob and following the horn.
  * The professor had arrived after midnight when no valet was present, left the key with a clerk, and never received a physical ticket.
  * When the professor later requested the car, staff required him to press several buttons on a phone before they would search for it.
* **Application**
  * The paid arrangement was a **mutual-benefit bailment**, so the hotel owed at least reasonable care.
  * Industry custom might bear on whether locating cars by the key-fob horn was reasonable, but custom would not excuse leaving the lights on and draining the battery.
  * Losing track of the car and leaving its lights on supported a finding that the hotel breached its duty of care.
  * Any purported electronic waiver faced serious contract-enforcement concerns because the professor lacked comprehension of the terms and was required to accept them in a coercive situation before the hotel would search for property already in its custody.
* **Conclusion**
  * The hotel likely breached the reasonable-care obligation owed as a compensated bailee, although the transcript did not quantify recoverable damages.

**Inter Vivos Gifts: Elements and Forms of Delivery**

* A valid **inter vivos gift** requires:
  1. **Present donative intent** to transfer ownership now.
  1. **Delivery** of the property or the relevant property interest.
  1. **Acceptance** by the donee.
* Acceptance is ordinarily uncontested in gift litigation because a claimant asserting ownership generally demonstrates a willingness to accept the property.
* Delivery may take three forms:
  1. **Actual delivery** occurs when the donor physically transfers the item.
  1. **Constructive delivery** occurs when the donor transfers the physical means of control, such as a car key or safe-deposit-box key.
  1. **Symbolic delivery** occurs through a signed writing identifying the property transferred, such as a writing giving the donee 1,000 shares of Apple stock.
* **Symbolic delivery** is particularly useful for intangible property or a property interest incapable of physical transfer.
* Gifts of real property similarly require **intent**, **delivery**, and **acceptance**, but a writing is required and functions as a form of symbolic delivery.
* Handing over a house key alone does not transfer title to land because keys are commonly transferred without any transfer of ownership.

**Present Gifts Versus Future or Testamentary Promises**

* Delivery helps distinguish “I am giving you my ring” from “I will give you my ring.”
* A promise to make a gift in the future is ordinarily unenforceable.
* A purported gift taking effect only at death is **testamentary** and generally must comply with the requirements for a will.
* Once a valid present gift is completed, the donor cannot unilaterally revoke it; the donee must validly transfer the property back.
* A prior deed hypothetical illustrated this point:
  * A mother executed and delivered a deed transferring property to her daughter.
  * When the daughter later handed the same deed back, title did not return to the mother because the instrument described only the mother-to-daughter conveyance.
  * A reverse transfer required a new valid deed from the daughter to the mother.

**Pearl-Ring Gift Hypotheticals**

* **Ring accidentally left at daughter’s home**
  * O accidentally leaves a pearl ring on A’s bathroom sink; the accidental act is not delivery because O lacked donative intent at that time.
  * When A later telephones, O says A may keep the ring as a gift.
  * Requiring A to return the ring merely so O could hand it back would be artificial and inconsistent with ordinary human behavior.
  * O’s telephone statement, combined with A’s existing possession, therefore completes a valid present gift.
  * O cannot demand the ring back the next day because ownership has passed to A, although A could voluntarily make a new gift back to O.
* **Dinner transfer and temporary return**
  * At dinner, O takes off the ring, hands it to A, and states, “I want you to have it. It’s yours.”
  * The statement and physical transfer establish **present intent** and **actual delivery**.
  * A’s discovery that the ring is too large does not reject the gift because A does not say that the ring is unwanted.
  * When O offers to wear it until A has it resized, O becomes A’s **bailee** rather than regaining ownership.
  * If O dies while wearing the ring, A remains the owner and may recover it from O’s executor, assuming A can prove those facts.
* **Promise effective at death**
  * If O instead says, “I promise to leave you this ring when I die,” the statement is an unenforceable future or **testamentary gift promise**.

**Symbolic Delivery When Actual Delivery Is Readily Available**

* If O is wearing a wristwatch and hands A a signed writing stating, “I hereby give A the wristwatch I am wearing,” traditional property law in most states does not treat the transaction as a completed gift.
* Although the writing resembles **symbolic delivery**, O’s failure to hand over an item immediately available for manual transfer suggests that no present transfer was intended.
* If the writing specified a definite present transfer of title with possession to follow at noon that day, it would probably be valid.
* When the donor’s behavior conflicts with the writing, courts may characterize the writing as a vague testamentary expression rather than enforce it as a present gift.
* The **Third Restatement** favors a more liberal interpretation, but the professor stated that courts generally have not adopted that approach.

**Safe-Deposit-Box and Bearer-Bond Hypothetical**

* Robert Hawks rented a safe-deposit box jointly with his sister Joan and intended to give her everything he placed in it.
* At a restaurant, Robert physically handed Joan four $5,000 bearer bonds and stated that he wanted to give them to her.
* Joan then placed those bonds in the box; because the gift was already completed through present intent and actual delivery, the four bonds remained hers.
* Robert later placed 22 additional bonds and a diamond ring in the box, remained the only person who actually entered the box, and continued clipping coupons and collecting interest.
* Robert placed a note in the box stating that its contents would belong to Joan upon his death and could be removed only by her.
* The note described a future transfer effective at death and therefore constituted an invalid **testamentary gift** that could not supersede the will.
* The 22 later bonds and ring were not validly gifted, while the four bonds actually delivered at the restaurant belonged to Joan.

**Gifts of Property Contained Within Other Property**

* A donor’s transfer of a container does not necessarily demonstrate intent to transfer a distinct, much more valuable item hidden inside it.
* Courts may require specific donative intent when:
  1. The contained item is readily understood as a separate property interest.
  1. The donor knew of and separately valued that interest.
  1. The contained item is substantially more valuable than the container.
* By contrast, a deed transferring land ordinarily transfers undisclosed coal, oil, or gold within the estate unless those interests have been separately severed.
* If a landowner separately owns the mineral rights and transfers only the surface estate, the distinct mineral estate does not pass merely because it lies under the conveyed land.
* The controlling comparison is whether the donor consciously recognized the disputed property as a separate interest requiring distinct intent.

**_Newman v. Bost_, North Carolina Court (1890s)**

* **Facts**
  * Van Pelt was a widower whose wife had died approximately ten years earlier.
  * After becoming paralyzed and confined to bed, he called for Enos Houston to nurse him during his final illness.
  * Julia Newman had lived with Van Pelt for approximately ten years and was described as his housekeeper, possible fiancée, or companion.
  * Shortly before his death, Van Pelt asked Julia to bring his private keys.
  * He told Julia that he wanted her to have everything in the house, pointed to a bureau, clock, and other furniture, had his bedroom door opened, and repeated that the property was hers.
  * One key opened a bureau drawer containing valuable papers, including a life-insurance policy worth substantially more than the bureau and the other property.
  * Julia retained the keys, announced her claim after Van Pelt’s death, and asserted ownership of the policy, a piano, household furniture, and the items in her own bedroom.
* **Procedural History**
  * A local jury broadly accepted Julia’s claim and awarded her the disputed property.
  * The higher court treated the testimony and claimed transfers more skeptically, partly because nothing was written, the evidence depended on testimony, and the local jury may have been sympathetic to Julia.
  * The piano issue was sent back for further proof concerning ownership or delivery.
* **Issue**
  * Did Van Pelt’s oral statements, Julia’s possession of the keys, and the locations of the items establish sufficient **donative intent** and **delivery** for each disputed item?
* **Holding**
  * No as to the life-insurance policy and household furniture for which neither manual nor effective constructive delivery was shown.
  * The furniture already located in Julia’s private room could be treated as previously delivered to her.
  * The piano claim required further proceedings, but appeared weak because Julia lacked dominion over the parlor and piano.
* **Reasoning**
  * Van Pelt never specifically mentioned the life-insurance policy.
  * His effort to give Julia the bureau did not necessarily establish intent to transfer a distinct policy worth much more than the furniture containing it.
  * Specific intent was especially important because Van Pelt had separately acquired and understood the policy as a valuable property interest.
  * Julia could easily have been instructed to remove the policy from the drawer, but Van Pelt did not give that instruction.
  * The key had value as a means of accessing the bureau itself, so giving the key did not necessarily symbolize delivery of every item inside.
  * **Constructive delivery** could apply to furniture specifically opened by the delivered keys, particularly where size and weight made manual delivery impractical.
  * A key did not constructively deliver furniture that the key did not open.
  * Items already in Julia’s private bedroom could have been delivered by placing them within her area of dominion after expressing intent that she own them.
  * Julia lacked comparable dominion over the piano in the common parlor.
  * If Julia and Van Pelt had been married or Julia had shared ownership or control of the house, placing the piano or furniture within that shared space would have provided stronger evidence of delivery.
  * North Carolina had not yet recognized **symbolic delivery**, but that doctrine might not have changed the outcome because Van Pelt left no writing.
* **Disposition**
  * The piano claim was remanded for additional proof; the transcript does not supply a single comprehensive disposition for every item.

**Constructive-Delivery Variations Following _Newman v. Bost_**

* **Specific policy identified but left in bureau**
  * If Van Pelt said, “I want to give you my insurance policy in that bureau; please get it,” but Julia or Enos left it there, the strict court would likely find no gift because manual delivery remained readily possible and never occurred.
* **Bureau physically moved to Julia’s room**
  * If Van Pelt ordered the bureau moved into Julia’s room while the policy remained inside, delivery of the bureau would be clearer.
  * The policy would still present an intent problem because the court could treat it as a distinct and far more valuable property interest.
  * If Julia expressly asked whether the policy was included and Van Pelt said yes, both specific intent and delivery would be much stronger.
* **Bureau and policy expressly identified; key transferred**
  * If Van Pelt expressly gave both the bureau and the policy locked inside and handed Julia the only key, **constructive delivery** would probably satisfy delivery because the bureau was too heavy for manual transfer.
* **Small strongbox variation**
  * If Van Pelt expressly gave Julia a three-pound strongbox and the policy within it but transferred only the key, many courts might uphold the gift because the key specifically controlled the box and its contents.
  * The strict court in _Newman_ would probably reject the gift because the lightweight box was readily capable of manual delivery.

**_Thomas_, Court and Year Not Supplied**

* The plaintiff in _Newman v. Bost_ relied on _Thomas_ as an example of effective constructive delivery.
* In _Thomas_, the articles were removed from the bureau drawer, and the delivered container or means of access was described as having little or no purpose apart from transferring the contents.
* _Newman_ was distinguishable because Van Pelt’s bureau had independent value and the life-insurance policy could easily have been removed and manually delivered.

**Gifts of Future Interests in Personal Property**

* A donor may separate ownership of personal property into a present **life estate** and a future **remainder interest**.
* A donor who keeps possession for life but presently and irrevocably transfers the remainder is making an **inter vivos gift** of a future interest, not merely promising a testamentary transfer.
* An **indefeasibly vested remainder** cannot be manually delivered because the donee has no present right to possession.
* **Symbolic delivery**, ordinarily through a writing, is therefore the only practical means of delivering such a future interest.
* The key analytical question is identifying exactly what property interest the donor intended to transfer; delivery must correspond to that interest rather than to immediate physical possession of the underlying chattel.

**_Gruen v. Gruen_, Court Not Supplied**

* **Facts**
  * In 1963, Victor Gruen wrote to his son Michael, then a Harvard student, concerning a Gustav Klimt painting as a twenty-first-birthday gift.
  * Victor’s first letter stated that he was giving Michael the painting while retaining possession and use during Victor’s lifetime.
  * At the advice of Victor’s lawyer and accountant, Victor sent a replacement letter omitting the retained-life-possession term to reduce inheritance-tax consequences.
  * A third letter explained that Victor still intended to use the painting during life, instructed Michael to return the first letter for destruction, and stated that the replacement documents were intended to permit Michael to receive the painting after Victor’s death without inheritance tax.
  * Michael destroyed the first letter but retained the third, which preserved evidence of Victor’s actual intent.
  * Victor kept and moved the painting among his homes until his death in 1980.
  * Michael never physically possessed the painting during Victor’s lifetime.
  * After Victor died, Michael’s stepmother, Kemija, possessed the painting and refused to surrender it.
* **Procedural History**
  * Michael sought a declaration that he was the painting’s rightful owner.
  * The trial court concluded that Michael had not established a valid **inter vivos gift**, reasoning that Victor’s retained possession made the attempted transfer testamentary.
  * The final reviewing court upheld the gift; the transcript does not provide the intervening appellate details or final court’s name.
* **Issue**
  * May a donor make a valid present **inter vivos gift** of a remainder interest in a chattel while retaining a possessory **life estate**, even though the donee receives no physical possession during the donor’s life?
* **Holding**
  * Yes. Victor presently transferred Michael an **indefeasibly vested remainder** while retaining a **life estate**, and the written communications provided the only delivery appropriate for that future interest.
* **Reasoning**
  * The sequence of letters unambiguously demonstrated Victor’s intent to make a present transfer of title while retaining lifetime possession.
  * Victor gave Michael ownership of the future interest rather than immediate possession of the painting.
  * Retention of a life estate did not make the transfer testamentary because Michael’s remainder vested during Victor’s life.
  * Actual delivery was impossible and unnecessary because a future interest carries no present possessory right.
  * The letters constituted **symbolic delivery** of the remainder.
  * If the surviving replacement letter alone had been treated as a gift of immediate ownership and possession, the gift would have failed because Victor never actually delivered the painting.
  * The third letter was therefore crucial because it established that the intended gift was a future interest consistent with Victor’s continued possession.
  * The court confined itself to determining whether the documents created a valid gift and left any alleged tax misconduct to the Internal Revenue Service and federal courts.
* **Policy**
  * Honoring the donor’s actual present intent supported recognition of future interests in valuable personal property.
  * The case established that the future-interest concepts applicable to real property can also operate with respect to personal property.
  * Jesse Dukeminier advised Michael to preserve the explanatory letter and later helped develop the future-interest theory that the court accepted.
